title: Sabena 548
summary: Sabena Flight 548, a Boeing 707 flying from New York to Brussels, made two aborted landing attempts at Brussels Airport on 15 February 1961 after a small aircraft had not yet cleared the runway. On a third circuit the aircraft's bank angle gradually increased until it reached a near-vertical bank at 1,500 ft; it then leveled its wings, pitched up abruptly, lost speed and spiraled nose-down into the ground near Berg, killing all 72 aboard and one person on the ground. Investigators could not conclusively determine the cause but believed the most likely explanation was a mechanical failure of the tail stabilizer-adjusting mechanism, possibly involving the wing spoilers.
probable_cause: The exact cause was never fully determined. Authorities agreed the most likely explanation was a mechanical failure of a flight-control mechanism, probably a malfunction of the wing spoilers or, as the FAA believed, the tail stabilizer-adjusting mechanism.

events.text: Near the runway threshold at a height of 900 ft, power was increased and the landing gear retracted after the approach was aborted because a small plane had not yet cleared the runway.
The 707 circled the airport and attempted to land on the adjoining Runway 25, which was not operational, but this second approach was also aborted.
Witnesses observed that the pilots were fighting for control of the aircraft, attempting to land despite a mechanical malfunction preventing a normal landing.
The plane's bank angle gradually increased until it had climbed to 1500 ft and was in a near vertical bank, then leveled its wings, pitched up abruptly, lost speed and spiraled rapidly, nose-down.
The plane plunged into the ground less than two miles from the airport at 10:05 CET, and eyewitnesses said it exploded and burst into flames.

notes: Cause was never conclusively established; text presents FAA's stabilizer-failure hypothesis as the leading theory among several considered.
